chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qasani, from Sulayman ibn Hafs al-Marwazi, from Abu al-Hasan al-Askari (peace be upon him) who said:

When the night reaches its midpoint, a whiteness appears in the middle of the sky resembling a pillar of iron, the world being illuminated by it. It lasts for a while, then disappears and darkness returns. Then when a third of the night remains, a whiteness appears from the eastern direction, illuminating the world. It lasts for a while, then disappears — and that is the time for the night salat. Then it darkens before dawn, then the true dawn rises from the east.
He said: 'And whoever wishes to pray the night salat at midnight, that is permissible for him.'

key_terms.الْفَجْرُ الصَّادِقُ: The true dawn (al-fajr al-sadiq) — distinguished from the false dawn (fajr al-kadhib), marks the beginning of Fajr prayer time
key_terms.بَيَاضٌ: Whiteness — the celestial sign used to determine divisions of the night for prayer timing purposes
key_terms.صَلَاةُ اللَّيْلِ: Night salat — the voluntary night prayer, a highly recommended act of worship performed in the last third of the night

ai.seo_question: When is the correct time to pray the night salat (salat al-layl) according to Imam al-Hadi?
ai.summary: Imam Ali al-Hadi (peace be upon him) describes two celestial signs that mark the divisions of the night: a pillar-like whiteness at midnight and an eastern glow when a third of the night remains. The latter marks the proper time for the night salat (salat al-layl). The Imam also permits performing the night salat at midnight for those who intend to do so, providing an important jurisprudential ruling on the flexibility of the prayer's timing. This narration was likely given to Sulayman ibn Hafs al-Marwazi, a direct companion of the Imam, who sought clarification on the correct astronomical signs for determining prayer times.
